source.title: Adaptive Textual Label Noise Learning based on Pre-trained Models
source.authors: Shaohuan Cheng; Wen-Yu Chen; Mingsheng Fu; Xuanting Xie; Hong Qu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports when clean and noisy text-label examples are learned during fine-tuning, a related test of V6 in a different task and setting.
record.gate_note: The paper tests learning order on simulated textual label noise. Its results do not test random image labels, fitting unstructured inputs, or the other claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own clean-versus-noisy label learning trajectories during standard cross-entropy fine-tuning of BERT on text classification. These results test V6 in a new setting, although most experiments evaluate a noise-mitigation method.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately describes the learning-order observation and its methodological role, but incompletely summarizes the conclusion. The authors conclude that adaptive warm-up followed by hybrid training prevents noisy-label overfitting and achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods across tested simulated noise settings. They acknowledge the absence of real textual-noise experiments and additional monitoring cost.
record.recipe_differences: Text classification with simulated class-conditional, instance-dependent, and mixed label noise; pre-trained BERT encoder plus a two-layer MLP. It does not use the original random-image-labeling setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper states that the optimal warm-up time varies across noise scenarios; for example, three epochs help with asymmetric noise while one epoch is enough for instance-dependent noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Noisy examples show predictions that fluctuate between the true and corrupted labels and are less consistently aligned with the supplied label.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: During fine-tuning on partially corrupted text datasets, predictions on noisy examples can alternate between their true and supplied labels.

record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2023
record.problems: The experiments use simulated noise rather than real textual noise. The reported learning-order evidence is qualitative in the text, and the paper does not test completely random labels or image inputs.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, near-zero training error under that labeling, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Time required to fit true versus completely random labels and convergence time across corruption fractions. Table 4 compares training methods under the same noise setting.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit throughout a corruption sweep from zero to complete randomization, together with steadily increasing test error toward chance. The reported test-accuracy comparisons at limited noise levels do not establish this joint claim.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent fitting completely random labels, and whether removing them alone harms clean-label generalization.

Completely random labeling and a direct comparison of wholly clean versus wholly random training sets; real-world textual noise. The demonstrated learning order concerns simulated corruption within partially noisy datasets.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the proposed V6 limits_scope verdict based on R2: untested completely random labels are an evidence gap, not an observed failure. The supplied text supports the qualitative learning-order finding but does not permit reliable numerical extraction of the plotted trajectories.

versions.untested_parts: Random labeling of the training set, training error, test error at chance, and unchanged architecture or hyperparameters.
Training time to fit true versus random labels and convergence as label corruption increases.
Perfect training fit and steadily rising test error across corruption levels while learning remaining signal.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent fitting random labels, and whether their removal harms true-label generalization.
The study examines simulated noisy labels, not completely random labels; it does not compare learning real labels with learning fully random labels.

rows.subject: BERT encoder and a two-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Measured the order in which clean and noisy training samples were recalled during learning.

conditions.value: different noise types; examples include class-conditional and instance-dependent noise

rows.measure: Relative timing of recall for clean versus noisy samples.
rows.value: The authors report that clean samples are recalled earlier than noisy samples during learning, regardless of noise type.
rows.note: The text states a qualitative result across noise types; it does not give per-condition values here.
rows.check: The qualitative learning-order result is correctly recorded. Specify the demonstrated settings: Figure 2 shows Trec with 40% asymmetric noise and Chnsenticorp with 40% instance-dependent noise; Appendix A, Figure 5 adds symmetric noise and other corruption levels. The observation concerns ordinary cross-entropy training trajectories, including later noisy-label fitting, rather than only the adaptively stopped warm-up.

rows.subject: BERT encoder and a two-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Examined prediction consistency with the given label for noisy samples during training.
rows.measure: Consistency of model predictions with the given noisy label.
rows.value: The authors report greater inconsistency with the given label for noisy samples, attributing it to activation of the true label.
rows.note: This reports a qualitative prediction pattern, not a direct comparison with training on random labels.
rows.check: Prediction inconsistency and switching between true and corrupted labels do not establish which labels are learned first. This is a related prediction-dynamics observation, not a partial manifestation or scope limitation of V6.

relationships.condition: BERT with a two-layer MLP, fine-tuned on text classification with simulated class-conditional or instance-dependent label noise
relationships.reason: R1 records the authors' empirical finding that clean-label recall rises before noisy-label recall, supporting signal-first learning in the illustrated settings.
relationships.display_finding: Clean-label recall rose before noisy-label recall in the illustrated classification settings.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Simulated textual label-noise settings examined during warm-up
reader_labels.reason: The authors report earlier recall of clean than noisy samples across noise types (R1), consistent with learning shared signal before noisy labels.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Prediction inconsistency with the given noisy label is reported, but the study does not test completely random labels or compare them directly with real labels (R2).
